content: Co-administration of tenofovir with drugs that impair renal function or compete for active tubular secretion can lead to increased serum concentrations of tenofovir. This interaction necessitates careful monitoring to avoid potential toxicity. Tolfenamic acid may increase the levels or effects of ganciclovir due to competition for renal tubular clearance by acidic (anionic) drugs. The clinical significance of this interaction is currently unknown but should be monitored. Similarly, tolmetin can elevate the levels or effects of ganciclovir through the same mechanism of competition for renal tubular clearance. The clinical relevance of this interaction is also uncertain and warrants observation. Trilaciclib, an OCT2, MATE1, and MATE-2K inhibitor, can decrease the levels or effects of ganciclovir. Co-administration of trilaciclib with substrates where even minimal increases in concentration could result in serious or life-threatening toxicities should be avoided. Alternative therapies are recommended in such cases. Ublituximab may reduce the efficacy of ganciclovir due to its immunosuppressive effects, increasing the risk of infections. Close monitoring is advised when these drugs are used together. Vadadustat can increase the levels or effects of ganciclovir through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Additionally, vadadustat may elevate the exposure of OAT3 substrates, necessitating monitoring for adverse effects and potential dose adjustments of the affected substrates. Ganciclovir can increase the levels or effects of valganciclovir due to competition for renal tubular clearance by acidic (anionic) drugs. The clinical significance of this interaction is not well established. Ganciclovir may enhance the toxicity of vinblastine, vincristine, and vincristine liposomal through pharmacodynamic synergy. The clinical importance of these interactions is uncertain but should be monitored. Co-administration of voclosporin and ganciclovir may increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Therapy modification and close monitoring are recommended in such cases. Willow bark may increase the levels or effects of ganciclovir due to competition for renal tubular clearance by acidic (anionic) drugs. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. Ganciclovir can increase the toxicity of zidovudine through pharmacodynamic synergy. This combination is contraindicated due to the potential for severe adverse effects. Ganciclovir is associated with a range of adverse effects, including hematologic toxicities such as thrombocytopenia, anemia, pancytopenia, and bone marrow failure. It can also cause elevated liver function tests, confusion, headache, nausea, vomiting, neuropathy, paresthesia, pruritus, retinal detachment, rash, sepsis, and weakness. Other reported effects include arrhythmias, tinnitus, visual impairment, gastrointestinal disturbances, fatigue, injection site reactions, hypersensitivity, infections, and renal dysfunction. Ganciclovir has been shown to cause mutagenesis and carcinogenesis in animal studies, with potential implications for human cancer risk. It may also impair fertility in both males and females and has been associated with fetal toxicity, including teratogenic effects, in animal studies. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants. Ganciclovir should be used with caution in patients with pre-existing cytopenias or those receiving myelosuppressive drugs or radiation. Hematologic toxicities, such as neutropenia, typically occur within the first two weeks of treatment but may resolve within 3-7 days after discontinuation. Colony-stimulating factors may help mitigate these effects. Renal impairment requires careful monitoring during ganciclovir therapy, as reduced renal clearance can lead to increased plasma concentrations and toxicity. Elderly patients and those receiving concomitant nephrotoxic medications are particularly at risk. Ganciclovir is not recommended for intramuscular, subcutaneous, or rapid intravenous administration due to the risk of increased toxicity. It should be administered via slow intravenous infusion over at least one hour at a final concentration not exceeding 10 mg/mL. Unused vials should be stored at room temperature (25°C or 77°F) and protected from freezing. Reconstituted vials should be stored at room temperature for no longer than 12 hours and should not be refrigerated or frozen. Diluted solutions should be refrigerated at 2-8°C (36-46°F) for no longer than 24 hours and should not be frozen. Ganciclovir is used to treat herpes infections of the eye but is not a cure for herpes. It is an antiviral medication that inhibits viral growth but does not eradicate the virus from the body. Proper application techniques and adherence to prescribed treatment duration are essential for optimal outcomes. Temporary blurred vision and mild eye irritation are common side effects. Serious allergic reactions are rare but require immediate medical attention. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies or pre-existing conditions before using ganciclovir. During pregnancy, the medication should only be used when clearly needed, and breastfeeding is not recommended. Drug interactions may alter the efficacy or safety of ganciclovir, so a comprehensive list of all medications and supplements should be shared with the healthcare provider. In case of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. Patients should adhere to prescribed dosages and schedules, and any missed doses should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is near the time for the next dose. Proper storage and disposal of the medication are essential to ensure safety and efficacy.
